nodes.bodyText:
🚀 Feature
This RFC is to upgrade MKL-DNN 0.20.1 to DNNL 1.1. DNNL is MKL-DNN's new name.  The major release DNNL 1.0 introduced a number of new features, and DNN 1.1 continues improvement on performance, quality, and usability. Below is an incomplete list, please refer to https://github.com/intel/mkl-dnn/releases for a full description.
DNNL 1.0 added SGEMM copy-based kernels for Intel SSE 4.1, Intel AVX, Intel AVX 2 and Intel AVX 512 architectures. With this optimization Intel MKL-DNN’ JIT SGEMM implementation achieves comparable performance to Intel MKL.

DNNL 1.0 introduced bfloat16 training and inference support in reorders, (de-)convolution, pooling, batch normalization, local response normalization, eltwise, inner product, shuffle, sum, and concat. The implementation relies on new instructions targeting future Intel Xeon Scalable processor (codename Cooper Lake). On Intel Xeon processors with Intel AVX512 support bfloat16 arithmetic is emulated.

DNNL 1.0 introduced Intel Processor Graphics support covering fp16 and fp32 inference, and fp32 training. Intel MKL-DNN relies on OpenCL* runtime to execute computations on Intel Processor Graphics and provides interoperability with user’s OpenCL code.

DNNL 1.1 includes (experimental) Introduced caching mechanism that reduces primitive creation time for repeated primitive creation. The functionality is disabled by default and has to be enabled in compile time.

Additional context
DNNL 1.0 comes with a new API design, but the most change is absorbed by ideep, the DNNL integration layer.  Below is a list of changes to Pytorch and Caffe2 to enable the DNNL 1.1.
	○ Build option change with new name (OMP:COMP vs. OMP)
	○ Implement ideep op using new DNNL operation (mul, add)
	○ Enable DNNL built-in primitive cache, remove hashing key to primitive cache in caffe2  
	○ change DNNL format representation (no explicit format tag like nchw). 
	○ Repalce passing allocator as op template with registering global allocator 
	○ Tensor construction code clean-up
	○ deconv IOHW workaround cleanup
	○ Simplify group conv interface

DNNL v1.1 PyTorch upgrade patch contains 3 components:
1. Upgrade underlying DNNL (original MKL-DNN) v0.21.1 to DNNL v1.1
2. Upgrade DNNL integration layer (iDeep)
3. Change build system and update PyTorch/Caffe2 integration
cc @VitalyFedyunin
nodes.title: upgrade MKL-DNN 0.20.1 to DNNL 1.1

This issue is created based on discussion with @jjlilley and @zzzwen. @pritamdamania87  and @aazzolini and I also encountered similar struggle in #30022 and pytorch/examples#662
Currently, application code needs to make sure there is no reference to UserRRef before calling join_rpc(), otherwise, those UserRRefs will be held alive by the application code and won't send messages to deref OwnerRRef. This would result in RRef leak errors. In our test and examples, we solve this by putting test/example code that involves RRefs into a separate function, and only call join_rpc() after exiting the function. When exiting the function scope, Python GC would deref the UserRRef is most cases. However, there are at least two problems with this approach:

Behavior is unclear when there are circular dependencies.
When the application code becomes complex, it is hard to track all RRefs and make sure they are de-referenced before calling join_rpc(). It would be a pain for application developers to debug and find dangling RRefs.

Proposal
Let's have a new arg in join_rpc()/shutdown() or even having a new API to specify whether we should nuke all local UserRRefs during shutdown. We can do this by:

Keep a weak_ptr to all UserRRefs in RRefContext, and use those to kill UserRRefs if necessary.
If UserRRef is destructed after nuke, do nothing.

cc @pietern @mrshenli @pritamdamania87 @zhaojuanmao @satgera @gqchen @aazzolini @rohan-varma @xush6528

Right now, some "Variable" functions are bound using native_functions.yaml, and some are not.  For example, Tensor::view() is manually bound on the Variable class, but Tensor::backward() is bound using native_functions.yaml. I thought, for uniformity sake, it would be better if all of these functions were bound on native_functions.yaml. But I cannot conveniently do this: when I do, ezyang@162e888 it fails with:
RuntimeError: is_view is not implemented for Tensor

The problem seems to be that my implementation strategy, which is defining an implementation on VariableType and then having it manually be registered as VariableTensorId, will result in a registered kernel that won't get called if variable mode is disabled. Being able to skip the variable implementation is desirable in the case of a function like add(), but for functions which have no reasonable non-variable implementation, like backward, we ought NOT to respect NonVariableTypeMode.
Does this mean we need a separate dispatch key for non toggleable variable implementations? Or maybe these should just be registered as composite ops. See also #29548

    self.up_4 = self.conv_block_2(self.num_filter*2, self.num_filter*1, act_fn)

    self.out = nn.Sequential(
        nn.Conv2d(self.num_filter, self.out_dim,  kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1), # 16, 1
        nn.Tanh(),
    )

def forward(self, input):
    # Encode
    down_1 = self.down_1(input)
    pool_1 = self.pool_1(down_1)
    down_2 = self.down_2(pool_1)
    pool_2 = self.pool_2(down_2)
    down_3 = self.down_3(pool_2)
    pool_3 = self.pool_3(down_3)
    down_4 = self.down_4(pool_3)
    pool_4 = self.pool_4(down_4)

    bridge = self.bridge(pool_4)

    # Decode
    trans_1 = self.trans_1(bridge)
    concat_1 = torch.cat([trans_1, down_4], dim=1)
    up_1 = self.up_1(concat_1)
    trans_2 = self.trans_2(up_1)
    concat_2 = torch.cat([trans_2, down_3], dim=1)
    up_2 = self.up_2(concat_2)
    trans_3 = self.trans_3(up_2)
    concat_3 = torch.cat([trans_3, down_2], dim=1)
    up_3 = self.up_3(concat_3)
    trans_4 = self.trans_4(up_3)
    concat_4 = torch.cat([trans_4, down_1], dim=1)
    up_4 = self.up_4(concat_4)

    out = self.out(up_4)

Intel Announced their new oneAPI to abstract the complexity of hardware acceleration away from higher-level libraries and code. I propose that PyTorch implements support for this, to bring hardware-accelerated GPU training to everyone who doesn't own an Nvidia® GPU.
